title: Presente Indicativo dei Verbi Regolari
subtitle: The present tense of -are, -ere and -ire verbs — Italian's three regular conjugations.
objectives: Conjugate regular -are, -ere and -ire verbs in the present tense
Recognize -isc- verbs, a common pattern within -ire
Use the present tense for habits, facts and (unlike English) near-future plans

content.intro: Every Italian verb belongs to one of three families, named for their infinitive ending: -are, -ere, -ire. Learn the pattern for one regular verb in each family, and you can conjugate hundreds of others the same way.
content.explanation:
To conjugate a regular verb, drop the infinitive ending (-are/-ere/-ire) and add the ending for each subject. A subgroup of -ire verbs (like capire, to understand) inserts -isc- before the ending in all forms except noi/voi — there's no way to predict which -ire verbs do this, so it's learned per verb.

The present tense also covers ground English splits into two tenses: Parlo italiano can mean both “I speak Italian” and, right now, “I am speaking Italian”. It's also commonly used for near-future plans: Domani parto per Roma (Tomorrow I'm leaving for Rome).

rules.heading: d) -isc- verbs (e.g. capire, finire, preferire, pulire)
rules.body: Same -ire endings, but -isc- is inserted before the ending for io/tu/lui-lei/loro: capisco, capisci, capisce, capiamo, capite, capiscono.

examples.en: You write a lot of emails.

examples.it: Lei dorme otto ore ogni notte.
examples.en: She sleeps eight hours every night.

commonMistakes.wrong: Io parlo l'italiano fluentemente da domani.
commonMistakes.right: Da domani parlerò... / Parlo italiano ora, ma da domani...
commonMistakes.why: Present tense for future plans works for near, planned events ("tomorrow I leave"), not for describing a change that will only become true later — that needs the future tense (covered at B1).
Capire is an -isc- verb: the io form is capisco, not a bare capo.
Noi always takes the -iamo ending, never the lui/lei -a/-e ending.

items.explanation: Noi never takes -isc-, even in an -isc- verb: capiamo.

items.prompt: Which is the correct io form of "finire"?
items.explanation: Finire is an -isc- verb: io finisco.
Capire needs -isc- in the io form: capisco.
Noi always uses -iamo, not a singular ending.

summary: Some -ire verbs insert -isc- before the ending, except for noi/voi.
The present tense covers habits, facts, right-now actions, and near-future plans.
